towards each other as God behaves, but it is equally foolish
to require that God should be determined in His action by
the principles which guide us. In order to illustrate the
character of God's action, Jesus narrates this story of the
householder and the labourers in the vineyard. In any event
the householder behaves quite correctly in so far as he faith-
fully gives to his labourers the agreed payment at the due
time. When those who were first hired complain that they
do not receive more, he is quite justified in his reply:
"Friend, I am doing you no wrong: did you not agree with
me for a denarius?" What proper answer can the grumbling
workman give? It is quite evident that the householder is
right; the labourer can raise no just claim.
And that is the first thing we are meant to learn from this
parable: man can raise no just claim in the sight of God.
God gives us what is our due, and no one has the right to
complain and require more. But the disposition to think that
we can make claims on God clings to us men and so often-
times we are accustomed to look at others who are faring
better than ourselves, and to complain: by what means have
they deserved better than we? Are there not many of these
lucky people who have toiled far less than ourselves? who
have endured far less trial and vexation? Yet they are to
fare better than we! With what justification? May we not
claim as much? Or else we moan: why am I in particular
struck by evil which is spared others? Yet they are no better
than I! In fact it is just those whose conduct is less exemplary
who so often escape! It is not seldom that thoughts and
feelings of this kind sway men's minds.
In fact it is this trend of thought which governs the
Jewish parable that has just been quoted. Its aim is to
comfort man with the doctrine that fundamentally God acts
in accordance with justice, i.e. justice as measured by the
standards of human justice, which rewards like performance
with like recompense. This parable rests on the conception
that God rewards the achievements of men, and hence must
give the same recompense to the same degree of merit. Now
